chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
title: Loew's Capitol Theatre demands an all-white band
summary: Near the end of the Second Herd, Loew's demanded an all-white orchestra at its Washington theatre; Herman sent the black players to New York for a week, then NAACP lawyers got involved, and Shelly Manne came in.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I had a band -- at this point, it was near the end of the Second Herd. And Shadow Wilson was on drums, and Oscar was still there, I believe -- I can't be positive about that. But Gene was and Ernie, and somebody else, I think.
No, it was right before Milt.
And we were to begin a theatre tour of eight weeks or ten weeks, which we needed. You need the dates because of the financial overhead.

And I got a notice from the Loews Booking Corporation with a tour of their theatres, and we were starting at their flagship house in Washington, D. C. at the Loew's Capital Theatre. I got a very heavy note from the management of that theatre and one of the big stockholders of the Loew's Corporation, that I would appear with an all-white orchestra in his
theatre or I would not appear there or the rest of the Lowe's Theatre tour.

There was no question of talking it over or listening to anybody's presentation, nothing. This was a statement of fact. So I didn't know what to do. I discussed it with my lawyers and -- before the tour. So I called the black guys to the dressing room, and I said, "Look, if we're going to finish this tour, which I certainly -- I know we have to, if we're going to continue," I said, "What I will do just so I can get over this thing about getting into the papers and everything else, without" "I said, "I will pay all your salaries plus expenses to go back to New York and have a ball for a week." We go to Indianapolis or (inaudible) whatever it is, right?

So the poor guys -- somebody talked to his wife or whoever. By the time they arrived and got off the train back in New York, there was a battery of lawyers from the NAACP and the whole thing. And they kept them up all night, grilling them, trying to do something for their people and the whole thing. P.S.: They were back the following morning. And it was pretty ridiculous kind of situation. And they said they didn't know why they were back, but were told it's (unintelligible) "Well, look, fellows, I'm not going to argue, you can do whatever you like, because it's bigger than I am. But I will tell you this: If you insist on staying here and going back to work, I'm certainly not going to prevent you. But I'll
tell you one thing, tomorrow morning I'll be back on my hill in California, and that's the end of me and this, " and --

So they snuck on back to New York, and we finished out the week. And I brought in to cope with this Shelley Mann situation -- that's when Shelley Mann came in the band. So they came in for a week, and then it turned out Shadow got zonked out and so Shelley stayed.
So did the other people ever come back then?

The people who'd been in the band? Yeah, sure, they came back and finished up the whole thing, as we had originally planned to do. But I could see the problems as far as themselves and their people and their friends, but mainly, it was -- if you want to do some propaganda, this was not the band to do it with, I don't think.
Because we were integrated, it was not (unintelligible).
It's just that Love's Incorporated was not integrated.
